newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian space officials to decide on Mir repairs.
newsitem.headline: Russian space officials to decide on Mir repairs.

text.p: The leading designers of Russia's space programme are due to make a formal decision on Monday on whether a new crew should try to carry out risky repairs to the damaged Mir space station.

Problems have plagued Mir's current mission since it was hit by a Progress cargo craft during a training docking on June 25, holing its Spektr module, damaging one of its solar panels and creating a power crisis on board.
Subsequently, an unidentified liquid leaked into space, million commander Vasily Tsibliyev suffered a heart problem and the onboard computer crashed when one of the crew pulled out a wrong cable.

Space officials have made clear that they think the current crew of Vasily Tsibliyev, Alexander Lazutkin and Michael Foale are too tired and too badly affected by stress to undertake the needed repairs.
"They have been through a lot, something which has a serious effect on a person's pyschology," mission director Vladimir Solovyov said in a television interview on Saturday.
Space officials have also said that cosmonauts Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov, due to arrive on Mir on August 7, are better trained for the repair job.

Solovyov said the planned meeting of designers would have the final say. Interfax news agency said the designers would meet in the Energiya company, a leading space rocket producer, situated near the Mission Control in Korolyov outside Moscow.

Repairing the power supply will require entering the airless module and working in spacesuits for several hours. If the operation goes wrong, officials say the crew doing the repairs may have to abandon ship.
Vinogradov and Solovyov are in training at Zvyozdny Gorodok outside Moscow to undertake the repair work and are due to blast off for Mir on August 5.

The problems on Mir, which was originally expected to have a usueful lifespan of about five years, have raised doubts about its future and that of Russian cooperation in space with the United States and other nations.
Asked if the United States would end its participation in the Mir project, U.S. President Bill Clinton said last Thursday that it was too soon for him to draw a conclusion.
